goal.what: The developers build and change the parts of the product so that together they deliver what the README promises the users.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers know what each part must do, for the users or for the product's development and operation, and why.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Solution strategy state first the one idea by which the product delivers what its README promises?
necessary_conditions.why: Each view carries out one idea, and a developer who knows the idea builds a part that serves it. The [solution strategy](https://docs.arc42.org/section-4/) of arc42 sums up first the few decisions that shape the whole.

items.text: Open your cut, and read to its end each input it names: the product vision, the README, and, where the product builds on another's rules, the architecture it builds on, such as a guide to building a plugin of the host it runs in.

In the README's How it works, take the first way it states, from the product vision's concept, by which the product brings its users to their objectives, such as keeping every decision of a run in one file that each role reads.
Ask how the system as a whole makes that way work: what it takes in from the roles, and what it turns that into, such as a request typed in a session turned into a deliverable that passed its checks.

Write the answer in two or three sentences that a developer can hold in mind while building any part. Point to the README instead of repeating it, and put it first in Solution strategy, before the rules that follow from it.

After writing the rest, read each component's line as a developer who knows only the idea, and check that they can see which piece of the idea it carries out. Change the idea or the component where they can't.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each user story state what a role wants, in the role's words and without the product's means, and do the stories together cover each objective of the product vision and each promise of the README?
necessary_conditions.why: The stories are the product's requirements: what each role wants, which the views then meet. A story that names a means, such as a command, states a design as a want, so no one asks whether the design serves the want. A [user story](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/user-stories) doesn't prescribe the solution, which the conversation and the acceptance criteria settle. Jeff Patton's [user story mapping](https://jpattonassociates.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/story_mapping.pdf) lays the role's activities along a backbone at one goal level, and hangs the stories on them, so a story covers what the use needs, not one step each.

items.text: Open the product vision and the README, and list each objective and each promise the README makes, in its walkthrough, its Non-goals, and its How it works.

For each objective, lay out as its backbone the activities its role does from where they start to the result they keep, read from the README's walkthrough for its main use. Name each in the words the role would say, such as approving the plan. A command or a screen of the product is no activity.

For each activity, ask what the role wants there and why, and write it as a story in the role's words, without a command, a screen, or a part of the product, since Sequences shows how the product meets it. One want often serves several activities, such as giving yes or a change at each sign-off.

Keep each story at the level of a goal the role reaches in one sitting, such as approving a deliverable, not a step within it, such as reading its changes, since stories at mixed levels leave gaps and overlaps that no one sees.

Read each idea of the product vision's Concept, and ask at which moment of the use it keeps the one way holding. Where the role wants something there that no story carries, add a story for it, such as going on with a run that stopped.
Where the product's development or operation wants something of the product, such as a release, write a story with the developer or the operator as its role.
For each objective and each promise, name the stories that carry it, and add a story where none does. Leave an activity without a story of its own where another story already carries it.

Read each story and ask whether it still holds where the product met it another way, such as a reply in place of a command. Rewrite each that doesn't, as it names a means, not a want, unless the role wants that means itself, such as working within the tool they already use.

necessary_conditions.about: Solution strategy, User stories, Components, Data model, Sequences
necessary_conditions.what: Does each rule of Solution strategy, user story, component, and kind of data trace to what the README promises the users, or to a need of the product's development or operation?
necessary_conditions.why: A part that nothing needs costs effort to build and to keep, and gives no one anything.

items.text: For each story, ask which activity, doubt, or need it carries, from three sources. The README and the product vision carry what the users get: the objectives and the promises that N2 lists, and the doubts that the README's How it works answers. Development adds what the developers need to build, test, and change the parts. Operation adds what keeps the product working across runs and updates, such as where its work outlives a run.
Once you have written Solution strategy, for each rule, name the doubt of the README's How it works, or the need of development or operation, that it carries.
Once you have drawn Sequences, for each component and each kind of data, find the rule or the step of a sequence that reaches it.
Remove each story or rule that carries none, and each component or kind of data that none reaches, from every figure, list, and sentence that names it.

critical_success_factors.what: Parts that different developers build fit together.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each rule of Solution strategy give a rule and a reason from which two developers decide a case that no line names the same way?
necessary_conditions.why: Developers of different parts meet the same kind of decision, and decide it apart unless a rule that every view follows settles it.

items.text: Derive the rules from the README's How it works, which answers each doubt of the users from an idea of the product vision's concept, and from the needs of development and operation.

For each answer and each need, ask what every part must hold alike for it to come true, such as where the work's state lives. A part that held it otherwise would break a key result. Each thing that every part must hold alike is a rule of Solution strategy.
Leave out what a single view already says, since a rule of Solution strategy holds only what spans the views.
For each rule, write it in one sentence, naming the parts as Components names them.

Write the reason in one sentence: what goes wrong without the rule, for a role of the product vision, naming the key result it guards, or for the developers or the operators. A developer carries the reason to a case that the rule doesn't name.
Where your cut names an architecture that the product builds on, point to its rules, and write only what this product adds or changes.
Take a case that no rule names, and decide it from each reason as two developers of different parts would. Where they differ, sharpen the reason.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each component state its responsibility, and does each decision that the stories need belong to exactly one component?
necessary_conditions.why: Two components that make the same decision make it twice, and the two copies drift apart. David Parnas's information hiding gives each module one decision that's hard to make or likely to change, and hides it from the rest.

items.text: Walk each story's steps, and name who acts at each: the role, a part of the product, or a thing outside the product. Each part of the product that acts is a component, of a kind that the architecture the product builds on offers where it offers kinds, such as a skill, a hook, or a script of a Claude Code plugin.
Take from the stories the decisions that are hard to make or likely to change, such as where the product keeps the work's state, or the form of a file that two parts share.

Give each decision to the one component that holds what it decides on, such as the form of the work's state to the component that writes the state. Where no component holds it, make a component for it.

Where another component needs the same decision, leave it with the component that holds it, and draw an arrow by which the other asks it, such as a hook that asks a script whether a step is done instead of reading the state itself.

Write under the figure each component's responsibility in one sentence: what the others expect it to do, the decisions it holds among it, such as `renders each page and sends what the user enters to the API`, so that a developer knows what to build and what to leave to the others.
Label each arrow with what one component does to another and the data it passes, not a word such as `uses`.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each component state its type and its technology?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who doesn't know what kind of thing a component is, or what it's built with, chooses alone, and the components stop fitting. The [C4 model](https://c4model.com/diagrams/container) gives each box its name, its type, such as a script, a skill, or a folder of JSON files, and its technology.

items.text: For each component, decide the type and the technology from the product's constraints, such as the runtime its users have.
Copy the template's skeleton of the figure to the deliverable's own, and place the boxes in the order the main story reaches them, left to right, so that its arrows run one way and cross no other.
Draw a store of data as a box like a component's, since its type sets it apart.
Give the figure a legend for every symbol.
Read the figure without the text around it, and add to the legend whatever symbol a reader would still have to ask about.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the data model show how each kind of data relates to the others, without its fields?
necessary_conditions.why: Two developers who build the writer and the reader of the same data must join it to the other data in the same way, while its fields stay free to change. A concept model in a class diagram of the Unified Modeling Language (UML), which most developers read, shows this.

items.text: Walk each story's steps and each arrow that Components draws, and list each kind of data that one component hands to another or that a store keeps, by the name the README gives it where it gives one, such as a run's record.
For each pair that relates, name the relation, and give how many of each it joins at both ends, such as a run that holds one or more rounds.
Draw each once, as a class by its name alone.
Where one holds the other's parts, put a filled diamond at the whole, since readers take a hollow one in different ways.
Group the data in a frame for each component or store that keeps them, in the order the stories meet them, with the data that most others join in the middle.
Leave the fields to where the developer builds the data.
Below the figure, say in a few words what a kind of data is only where a reader could take its name for another's.

necessary_conditions.about: User stories, Components, Data model, Sequences
necessary_conditions.what: Does each user story have a sequence that shows, at each step, which component acts, along which arrow, and with which data?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer building a step must know who acts there, on what, and what comes next. A [UML](https://www.omg.org/spec/UML) sequence diagram draws a story's steps in order, from the role's first request to what the story gives them.

items.text: For each story, draw each step as a message from one component to another along an arrow of Components, with the data it passes, named as in the data model.

At each step, ask what can go otherwise there, from the README's walkthrough and from what each component alone decides: an input that a component refuses, a check that fails, or a choice that only the role can make, such as a question that the walkthrough shows the role answering.

Draw an input refused as a branch, a check that fails as a step that sends work back to the step it repeats, and a choice of the role as a question put to the role with its answers, since each path of the story, and its integration test, rests on them.
Let stories that share their steps share a diagram.

Read each sequence as the developer who builds one of its steps, and check that they can tell, at each step, which component acts, along which arrow of Components, with which data, and what comes next. Where no arrow carries a step, add the arrow, or give the step to another component.

necessary_conditions.what: Do the figures, lists, and sentences agree with one another, and with the architecture that the product builds on, on what each part does?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who finds two places that say different things about a part must choose which to follow, and two developers choose differently.

items.text: For each part, gather what every figure, list, and sentence says it does, and, where your cut names an architecture that the product builds on, what each of its rules asks of a part of that kind, such as a rule that every hook gives its result as JSON.
Where two disagree, decide by the reasons of the rules of Solution strategy and of those of the architecture it builds on which is right, and change the other.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers can place, set up, and start every part without asking anyone.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Deployment show where each component runs, where the product keeps each kind of data, and how the product starts?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer setting up the product needs to know where each part runs, what it can reach, and how it starts. A [C4 deployment diagram](https://c4model.com/diagrams/deployment) shows this.

items.text: List each environment the product runs in, such as the user's computer or CI, with its technology.
Place each component and each kind of data in one deployment unit within its environment, such as the plugin's folder that the host installs, or the run's folder in the user's repository.
Add each thing outside the product that the components depend on, with what they use of it, and no infrastructure that they don't need.
Write in one sentence how the product starts.
Check that a developer could set the product up from nothing by the figure and that sentence.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each component and each kind of data have one place for its files?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer making a change must find the one place it belongs. Simon Brown's package by component, in Robert C. Martin's *Clean Architecture*, lays out the code by the components that the architecture draws.

items.text: Lay out the folders by component, so that each component and each kind of data has its own place, such as a folder for the hooks and one for the code they call.
Say in one sentence for each top folder whom its files are for, such as the users who install the product or only its developers.
Show each folder and file that holds a component or a kind of data, by its real name, one line each, nested as on disk, without the files inside a component.
Beside each, say what it does or holds, in the words a developer looks for when making a change.
Check that, for any change to a component, a developer can name the one folder it goes in.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers find each gap between the parts before they build any part, and know, as they build, that the product does what the document and the product vision say.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Test strategy give only the checks that the product's purpose needs, picked from the test strategy guide, each with its test target, and for a quality its tool and criterion, or for a benchmark its tool and what it measures?
necessary_conditions.why: A failure that no test looks for reaches the users unseen, and a case's pass or fail decides the work only where its criterion is set before anyone writes it. Where a result varies from run to run, as a prompt's does, a criterion passes or fails by chance, so a benchmark measures it and a person decides. A row for every check of the guide decides nothing for most of them, so Test strategy holds only the types the product's purpose needs.

items.text: Read [the test strategy guide](test-strategy-guide.md) to its end.

Take each check's test target from the guide. Unit tests try the parts against their contracts, each prompt among them. Integration tests try the parts joined against each element of this document. End-to-end (E2E) tests try the product in real use against each key result of the product vision. Use no other name for a test, so that each case's level tells which target it checks.

Pick each check that the guide says to pick always, and each other check whose condition the product meets, given what it is and what it builds on, such as a contract test where the tests use a double of a host that changes on its own schedule. Write no row for a check left out.
Make each check a benchmark where its test's path runs a prompt, as the guide's rule says, and each other check as the guide gives it.
For each check the product runs, choose its tool from the product's constraints, such as the runtime its users have, and name it.

Take each quality's criterion that the guide recommends, or the one that the architecture the product builds on sets. Change it only where the product can't meet it, or a key result needs more, and say why in the row.
For each benchmark, name what it measures, such as a key result or each case's results over several runs of a prompt. Set no criterion, as a person judges from the results.

Set how many times a benchmark runs each case by its first runs: add runs until one more no longer changes what the results show, such as the mean of a key result by a step of its measure, since the AI's variance shows only across runs. Where the product can't run yet, write this rule in place of the number, for the first run to set it.

For the trace of the architecture, set as the criterion that every element of this document, each story, rule, component, and kind of data, has an integration test, and that every test names an element or a case one level up that exists. Name the script that checks this by the names of the elements, not by reading, since only a check by name finds each element that no test reaches.
Write one row for each check picked, in the guide's order, in the template's table. Give each its kind as the guide or the prompt rule makes it.

necessary_conditions.what: Is each gap that the software design and the test design found from the document mended in it, so that the two designs, made again from it, find none?
necessary_conditions.why: A skeleton of the parts and test cases through it, made from the document before any body is built, show each gap between the parts while it's still cheap to mend: a case that no part can hold, or a handoff that no interface carries. Each gap mended in the document, not in the code around it, keeps the document true for each developer who builds on it.

items.text: Once Test strategy names the tools, have the skeleton made from the document by [the software design best practice](../software-design/best-practice.md), and then the test cases by [the test design best practice](../test-design/best-practice.md), each with its list of gaps.

For each gap that the lists name, change the document: give a case a part, or a decision a component; remove a part that no case reaches, as N3 says; split a component by its decisions or its reasons to change; and give a handoff an arrow and a kind of data.
Have the two designs follow the changed document as their practices say, and mend each gap they list again, until they list none.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each thing that the document says the product does rest on a part that a unit or integration test can check?
necessary_conditions.why: The E2E tests are slow and few, so they can only confirm what the lower levels already showed, and a thing that only a prompt holds varies from run to run, where only many runs on the model show it. The [Humble Object](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/HumbleObject.html) pattern of Gerard Meszaros's *xUnit Test Patterns* moves the logic out of a part that's hard to test into a part that a test can run.

items.text: For each thing the document says the product does, name the part that holds it.
Where only a prompt holds a rule that must hold on every run, give the rule to a part that a test can run, such as a guard of the architecture the product builds on, and draw that part in Components.
Leave a judgment that only an AI can make, such as whether a point is the user's, with the AI, and measure it by the prompt's unit tests on the model, as N12.8 sets.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers can change the product without making the document wrong.

necessary_conditions.about: Components, Data model, Sequences, Deployment, Directory structure
necessary_conditions.what: Does each view give each decision that a key result rests on, with its intent?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who doubts a decision and can't see what it was for may undo it and bring back the problem it solved. An [architecture decision record](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), by Michael Nygard, keeps a decision with its context, and its intent is what a developer needs to keep it.

items.text: For each view, take each decision that a key result rests on, such as a technology, a tool, or the form of a file that two parts share, and ask why it's taken, ending with the key result it serves.
Write each under its view's Strategies: the decision in a few words, and its intent in one sentence.
Leave out a decision that no key result rests on, since its intent gives a developer nothing to keep.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the document hold only what stays true while the product vision and Solution strategy stay, and leave each component's internals out?
necessary_conditions.why: A line about how a component works inside becomes untrue at the next change to that component, and the developer then can't trust the document. David Parnas's [information hiding](https://doi.org/10.1145/361598.361623) keeps such details inside the module.

items.text: For each line, ask whether it would become untrue if a component's internals changed while the product vision and Solution strategy stayed.
If it would, move it to where the developer builds the component.

Imagine a change to how a component works inside, such as its steps, a value it uses, or a data's fields, and mark each line it would make untrue. Repeat with a change of another kind until you mark no line.
